name: Dani Ortega
bio: Dani Ortega has been banned from Starlight Mall four times and has come back five. She skates the drained fountain in the dead wing, knows every service corridor and loose ceiling tile, and can rebuild a cracked deck with nothing but duct tape and spite. She is loud, fearless and very funny, especially when she is scared, which she will never admit. She has a hopeless crush on the girl who works the Corn Dog Corral counter and has been 'about to talk to her' since August. Her flaw is that she would rather eat concrete than ask for help, and she picks fights with things twice her size because somebody has to.

perk.name: Fountain Diver
perk.text: Dani skates the dead wing's dry fountain every morning and pockets whatever the mall rats dropped: +1 quarter each dawn.

meet.title: The Dead Wing Ramp
meet.place: The dead wing, Starlight Mall
meet.text: Behind the arcade, past a sawhorse that says CLOSED FOR RENOVATION since 1984, a girl with a hot-pink undercut is carving the drained fountain while a security guard named Gus wheezes after her. She shoots past you, flips you a roll of duct tape and hisses, "Hold this. You never saw me." Then she vanishes up a pillar. Gus is coming around the corner, and her board is still spinning in the fountain.
meet.art: A drained mall fountain in a dusty, half-lit dead wing, a skateboard spinning upside down in the basin, a pink-haired skater clinging to a pillar above, a heavyset security guard rounding the corner

choices.label: Send Gus running with a fake lost-kid emergency

success.text: "My little brother's in the food court and he's eating a whole Orange Swirl cup with a FORK!" Gus lumbers off at full speed. Dani drops from the pillar and stares at you. "You lie like a professional. Okay. You're in."
success.art: A pink-haired skater dropping down from a mall pillar, laughing and pointing at a teenager, a security guard running away in the distance

failure.text: Gus squints at you, then at the spinning skateboard, then at the duct tape in your hand. You're both marched out the side door. In the parking lot Dani is cackling. "Loading dock's unlocked tomorrow. Same time."
failure.art: Two teenagers sitting on a curb in an empty mall parking lot, one holding a skateboard and laughing, a mall security door slammed behind them

choices.label: Grab her board and drop into the fountain

success.text: You drop in, wobble, nearly die, and somehow carve all the way around the fountain and out the other side. Dani whoops so loud a pigeon falls off a light fixture. "That was the ugliest thing I've ever seen. Do it again. You're with me now."
success.art: A teenager wobbling through a drained mall fountain on a pink skateboard, a pink-haired skater whooping on the rim, a startled pigeon mid-flight

failure.text: You eat it hard. Dani slides down, peels a strip of duct tape and slaps it over the rip in your sleeve like a field medic. "Rule one, learn to fall. Come back tomorrow, I'll teach you." Gus's flashlight finds you both.
failure.art: A pink-haired skater kneeling to duct-tape a fallen teenager's torn sleeve inside a dry fountain, a security flashlight beam sweeping toward them

choices.label: Help her fix the cracked deck before Gus finds it

success.text: You show her how to lay the tape crosswise so the crack can't spread. She tests it with one stomp and grins. "Okay, genius. Anybody who can fix a board can come with me." She splits the change she found in the fountain with you.
success.art: Two teenagers crouched behind a planter, crisscrossing silver duct tape over a cracked skateboard, coins scattered on the tile

failure.text: The tape sticks to everything: the board, your hair, Dani's flannel, a passing pigeon. Gus finds you both in one glittering silver knot. Dani is laughing too hard to run. "Tomorrow," she wheezes. "Bring scissors."
failure.art: Two teenagers hopelessly tangled together in silver duct tape beside a cracked skateboard, a security guard standing over them with his hands on his hips

name: Marcus "Mix" Bell
bio: Marcus Bell got the midnight-to-six shift at KGLM because the last overnight DJ quit after something breathed on the call-in line, and Mix has never been happier. He runs the board, does his calculus between songs, and talks to the whole sleeping valley in a voice like warm velvet. He can name the label, year and B-side of almost any record ever pressed, and he notices instantly when a song plays wrong. On air he is smooth and fearless; in person he is shyer than he lets on, a little vain about his record collection, and secretly afraid nobody is really listening. He wants to program a station in Oakland someday and play everything.

perk.name: Dawn Dedication
perk.text: Every sunrise, Mix plays a song for you on the air, by name, no matter what happened in the night: +1 nerve each dawn.

meet.title: Dead Air
meet.place: The KGLM 103.3 booth at the base of the water tower
meet.text: The KGLM booth is a cinderblock box under the water tower, papered with album covers. Mix Bell is supposed to be asleep before his overnight shift, but he is hunched over the request line, receiver to his ear. "Every afternoon at three," he whispers, "somebody calls and hums a song. Same song. I know every record in this building and I don't know this one." He holds out the receiver. A girl is humming a slow dance, very sweetly, from very far away.
meet.art: A cramped radio booth papered with album covers, a teenage DJ in a purple satin jacket holding out a telephone receiver, sunlight slanting through a small window, a water tower visible outside

choices.label: Listen hard and name the song she is humming

success.text: "'Moon Over Crystal Springs,'" you say. "The slow dance from the old prom records." Mix stares, then dives into the archive and comes up with a dusty 1966 single. "Nobody knows that record. NOBODY." He presses a mixtape into your hands. "You're on my crew now."
success.art: A teenage DJ holding up a dusty vintage 45 record in triumph inside a radio archive, a teenager beside him holding a cassette mixtape

failure.text: You guess a song from a cereal commercial. The humming stops. The caller laughs softly and hangs up, and the turntable behind you starts spinning on its own, empty. Mix lifts the needle with a shaking hand. "Come back tomorrow. I'm finding this record if it kills me."
failure.art: An empty turntable spinning by itself in a radio booth, a teenage DJ reaching for the tone arm, a telephone receiver dangling off its hook

choices.label: Grab the mic and fill the dead air with a fake weather report

success.text: "Tonight in Glimmer Falls, clear skies, light fog, and a ninety percent chance of something in your closet." Mix laughs so hard he has to mute the board. "Okay, you've got a radio voice. You're coming on my show. And my crew. Mostly my crew."
success.art: A teenager speaking dramatically into a studio microphone while a teenage DJ doubles over laughing at the mixing board, an ON AIR sign glowing

failure.text: You open your mouth and nothing comes out. The microphone squeals with feedback that sounds almost like a scream, and the station manager bangs on the glass. Mix mouths "tomorrow" and gives you a thumbs-up you don't deserve.
failure.art: A frozen teenager in front of a squealing microphone, a red-faced station manager pounding on the booth window, a DJ giving a sympathetic thumbs-up

choices.label: Trace the call on the old station switchboard

success.text: You follow the lit line through a nest of cables to a number Mix looks up in the phone book. It belongs to a pay phone in the old Glimmer Falls High gym, disconnected in 1966. Mix whistles low. "Okay. You and me are figuring this out together."
success.art: Two teenagers bent over an old switchboard with tangled cables, a phone book open between them, one finger on a listing for a gymnasium pay phone

failure.text: You pull the wrong cable. Every line on the board lights up at once, and from every receiver comes the same slow breathing. Mix yanks the power cord. In the silence he says, very calmly, "New rule. Come back tomorrow, when it is more daylight."
failure.art: A radio switchboard with every button lit up red, a dozen phone receivers off their hooks, a DJ yanking a power cord from the wall

name: Delphine Hart
role: Head librarian and keeper of the town record
bio: Delphine Hart rides a cherry-red 1971 motorcycle to work, wears cardigans like armor, and knows exactly where every lie in Glimmer Falls is filed. She kept the occult stacks open when the library board wanted them locked, and she shushes people with a look that could stop a werewolf. In 1966 she was eighteen and in love with Roz Vance, the prom queen, and on prom night Roz was taken from her by a cruel prank the town decided to forget. Delphine still wears the ring they bought each other at the county fair. She is dry, deadpan, guarded and quietly furious, and twenty years of grief have taught her to answer every question but the ones about herself.

perk.name: Card Catalog Mind
perk.text: Delphine knows where every story in this town is shelved: the case board shows your odds of finding each clue.

meet.title: Boxing Up the Occult
meet.place: The occult stacks, Glimmer Falls Public Library
meet.text: A memo from the library board is taped to the end of the occult stacks: REMOVE ALL MATERIALS BEFORE HALLOWEEN. Ms. Hart is packing them into banker's boxes as slowly as a person can pack anything. She does not look up. "If you're here for the Stephen Kingsley, it's checked out until 1990," she says. On the cart beside her is a 1966 yearbook, and her thumb keeps turning a silver ring around and around.
meet.art: A librarian in an oxblood cardigan slowly packing occult books into cardboard boxes between tall shelves, a typed memo taped to the shelf end, a 1966 yearbook on a book cart

choices.label: Help her 'lose' the most important books before the board comes back

success.text: You slide the best grimoires behind the encyclopedias in the children's section, spine-in. Ms. Hart watches you work, and for the first time something like a smile crosses her face. "The board never goes into the picture-book room. You have instincts. Come by after closing."
success.art: A teenager sliding old leather books behind a row of children's encyclopedias in a colorful kids' section, a librarian watching with a faint smile

failure.text: A board member in a pastel suit catches you with three grimoires under your shirt. Ms. Hart takes the blame instantly and coldly. Later, on your way out, she murmurs without looking at you, "Come back tomorrow. Bring a bigger backpack."
failure.art: A stern woman in a pastel suit pointing at a teenager holding stacks of old books, a librarian stepping between them

choices.label: Ask, gently, about the ring she keeps turning

success.text: She is quiet a long time. Then she opens the yearbook to a girl with a cloud of dark hair and a laugh you can see from twenty years away. "Rosalind Vance. Roz. She could dance like gravity was optional." She closes the book softly. "I've never said her name out loud in this building. Thank you."
success.art: A librarian showing a teenager a black-and-white 1966 yearbook photo of a laughing girl, a silver ring catching the lamp light

failure.text: Her face closes like a book. "That's private." The lights in the aisle flicker, and from somewhere deep in the stacks comes the scratch of a needle on an old record. She goes white and turns away. "Maybe tomorrow, kid."
failure.art: A librarian turning her back in a dim library aisle as the overhead lights flicker, a teenager standing alone among the shelves

choices.label: Find the book she has been hunting for in the uncatalogued shelves

success.text: Misshelved under DEMONOLOGY you find the 1966 Glimmer Falls High prom program, a dried blue petal pressed inside. Ms. Hart takes it with both hands. "I've been looking for this for twenty years." She clears her throat. "You're useful. That's the highest compliment I give."
success.art: A teenager holding out a faded prom program with a pressed blue petal to a librarian between dusty shelves

failure.text: The uncatalogued shelves lean in like they are reading over your shoulder. A book leaps off the top shelf and lands open at your feet on a page of nothing but the word STAY. Ms. Hart shelves it with a snap. "That one bites. Come back tomorrow."
failure.art: A heavy book lying open on a library floor with a single repeated word filling its pages, shelves leaning ominously over a startled teenager

name: Toby Nakamura
bio: Toby Nakamura is shooting his masterpiece, Attack of the Cul-de-Sac, on a shoulder camcorder he borrowed from the AV club in September and has not returned. He works weekends at Rewind Video rewinding returns for store credit, knows four recipes for fake blood, and can tell you how every effect in every monster movie was done. His grandmother tells him ghost stories from Hiroshima prefecture over tea; his father thinks horror movies are a waste of a good mind. Toby's flaw is that he would rather film the monster than run from it, and he directs his friends like they are his cast. He is sweet, intense, a little bossy, and braver behind a lens than anywhere else.

perk.name: Take Two
perk.text: Toby yells "cut!" and everybody resets: reroll one failed daytime roll each day.

meet.title: Extra Wanted
meet.place: The horror aisle, Rewind Video
meet.text: In the horror aisle of Rewind Video, a kid in a yellow windbreaker has taped an X to the carpet and is lying on his back, filming up at the shelf of slasher tapes. "I need a scream," he announces to nobody. "A real one. Mine sounds like a teakettle." He spots you. "You. You have a screaming face. Also, my tape from last night came out weird and I think I filmed something I didn't film."
meet.art: A teenage boy in a yellow windbreaker lying on the carpet of a video store horror aisle, pointing a shoulder camcorder up at shelves of lurid VHS boxes, a tape X marked on the floor

choices.label: Hit the mark and give him a classic scream-queen scream

success.text: You throw your hands to your face and let rip. The whole store goes silent. From the counter, the old clerk applauds slowly. Toby lowers the camera, awed. "That's a take. That's a PRINT. You're in my movie. You're in my crew."
success.art: A teenager screaming dramatically on a tape mark in a video store aisle, a boy filming with a camcorder, an elderly clerk applauding from the counter

failure.text: Your scream cracks into a squeak halfway through. Two kids in the comedy aisle laugh. Toby pats your shoulder with total sincerity. "No, that was honest. Honest is good. We'll reshoot tomorrow."
failure.art: A blushing teenager in a video store aisle, two kids snickering behind a shelf, a boy with a camcorder giving an earnest thumbs-up

choices.label: Help him rescue the tape the store VCR ate

success.text: You wind the crinkled tape back with a pencil and play it in the back room. There is Crystal Street at 3 a.m., and in the corner of the frame a tall shape in curlers, walking through a front door without opening it. Toby whispers, "We're going to need a bigger crew. You're it."
success.art: Two teenagers in a cluttered video store back room staring at a small TV showing grainy night footage of a suburban street and a shadowy tall figure

failure.text: The VCR eats your sleeve too. When you finally pull free, the screen shows one frame of you, asleep in a pink salon chair you have never sat in. Toby ejects the tape very carefully. "Okay. Tomorrow. We look at this tomorrow."
failure.art: A small TV in a dark back room frozen on a grainy still of a teenager asleep in a pink salon chair, a jammed VCR chewing a sleeve

choices.label: Distract the manager so Toby can film in the stockroom

success.text: You ask the manager to explain the difference between Beta and VHS, and he gives you twenty uninterrupted minutes. Toby emerges from the stockroom glowing, with a cardboard cutout of a swamp monster under his arm. "You're a natural producer. Welcome aboard."
success.art: A video store manager lecturing a teenager while gesturing at two tape formats, a boy sneaking out of a stockroom behind them with a cardboard monster cutout

failure.text: The manager sees straight through you and catches Toby elbow-deep in the stockroom. You're both sent out to the curb. Toby, unbothered, films the sunset. "Rejection builds character. Come back tomorrow. I'll storyboard it."
failure.art: Two teenagers sitting on a curb outside a neon video store at sunset, one filming the sky with a camcorder

name: Glory Hallelujah
pronouns: she/her in drag, he/him out of it (Gordon)
role: Drag queen and revue mother of the Glitter Box
bio: Out of drag he is Gordon Pike, who keeps the Glitter Box's books, teaches Tuesday tap, and fixes the boiler with a wrench and a prayer. In drag she is Glory Hallelujah, six-foot-four in heels, sequins and steel, mother of the Saturday revue and of every stray kid who wanders in looking for somewhere to be themselves. In 1961, nineteen-year-old Gordon sat in Frieda Krueger's salon chair and got his first real haircut, and Frieda told him to be bold. Glory has been bold ever since. She is devastatingly funny, generous to a fault, and keeps a grudge like a scrapbook. Her flaw is that she will turn any hurt into a punchline before she lets anyone see it land.

perk.name: Mother's Morning Read
perk.text: Glory calls at dawn to tell you exactly how fabulous you were last night: +1 nerve each dawn.

meet.title: The Closing Number
meet.place: Backstage, the Glitter Box Playhouse
meet.text: Backstage at the Glitter Box smells of hairspray, mothballs and fresh coffee. A towering queen in a half-zipped magenta gown is pacing between racks of costumes. "Bunny dropped out. Nightmares, she says, every night, somebody trying to cut her hair." She whirls on you, takes you in from shoes to scalp, and her eyes stop on a single gray streak in your hair you didn't have last week. Her face changes. "Well," Glory says softly. "Sit down, sugar."
meet.art: A towering drag queen in a magenta sequin gown pacing backstage among costume racks and lighted mirrors, a teenager standing by the stage door, a single gray streak in the teenager's hair

choices.label: Learn Bunny's closing number in one afternoon

success.text: Kick, turn, fan, dip, and you hit the final pose exactly on the cymbal. The chorus erupts. Glory dabs her eyes with a glove. "Mother is weeping. Somebody put this child on the bill, and somebody get this child on my crew."
success.art: A teenager striking a dramatic final pose on a small stage while a chorus of drag performers cheers, a tall queen dabbing her eyes with a gold glove

failure.text: You turn left on the kick and land in the orchestra pit, which is one upright piano. Glory hauls you out by the collar. "Tomorrow, same time. Bring sneakers, not ambition." She is laughing, which helps.
failure.art: A teenager tangled on top of an upright piano below a small stage, a drag queen in sequins leaning down laughing with an outstretched hand

choices.label: Tell her about the salon chair in your dreams

success.text: When you mention the shears, Glory sits down hard on a costume trunk. "Frieda Krueger cut my hair in 1961. Told me to be bold." She takes your hand. "Whatever's wearing her face now, she was kind to me once. We are going to figure this out together, you and Mother."
success.art: A drag queen sitting on a costume trunk holding a teenager's hand, an old salon appointment card on her knee, dressing-room bulbs glowing

failure.text: Glory laughs too loudly and too long and changes the subject to wigs. She sends you off with a hug that is a little too tight. On the bus home you find a long silver hair on your sleeve that isn't yours. Come back tomorrow; she'll be ready.
failure.art: A teenager on a city bus at dusk picking a single long silver hair off their sleeve, the glowing marquee of a small theatre receding through the window

choices.label: Help the costume crew mend a torn gown before curtain

success.text: You hold the seam while the crew stitches, and you find the loose sequins nobody else could. Glory zips into the gown, twirls, and points at you with a gloved finger. "This one stays. Anybody who saves a gown is family."
success.art: A drag queen twirling in a repaired sequin gown backstage, a teenager holding a spool of thread and grinning, sequins glittering in the air

failure.text: You sew the gown to your own jeans. Twice. Glitter gets in places glitter should not be. Glory snips you free with great dignity. "Darling, come back tomorrow, and come back without a needle."
failure.art: A teenager accidentally stitched to a magenta sequin gown, a drag queen snipping the thread with tiny gold scissors, glitter everywhere

name: Frankie Fontaine
bio: Frankie Fontaine came up from Fresno at nineteen with a suitcase, a toolbox and a new name she had picked out at fourteen, and Glory Hallelujah handed her a headset the same night. Five years later she runs the Glitter Box: the fly system, the projector, the fog machine, the fuse box that should have been condemned in 1974. On Saturdays she hosts the midnight double feature as Frankie Fright, in a lab coat and a beehive, heckling the screen. She can rig anything from a pulley and gaffer tape. She is sarcastic, organized to the minute, and terrible at resting; her flaw is that she carries everyone's problems and forgets to set them down, and she would rather rewire a building than say she is tired.

perk.name: Safety Line
perk.text: Frankie rigs a harness for everything: once per night, cancel the nerve loss from one failed roll.

meet.title: The Extra Frame
meet.place: The projection booth, the Glitter Box Playhouse
meet.text: The projection booth is a hot little box full of film cans and fuses. A woman in a headset is halfway up a ladder rewiring the projector lamp, a pencil in her teeth. "Don't touch anything," Frankie Fontaine says around it. "Last Saturday, in the middle of the second feature, somebody spliced a frame into my reel. One frame. Everybody in the house screamed and nobody could say why." She points with her pliers at a reel on the rewind bench.
meet.art: A cramped theatre projection booth full of film cans, a woman in a headset on a ladder rewiring a big film projector, a film reel resting on a rewind bench in a pool of lamp light

choices.label: Hold the ladder and pass her the right tools

success.text: Wire strippers, needle-nose, the blue tape, not the black. You're one step ahead every time. Frankie climbs down and looks at you like you're a new piece of equipment she didn't know she needed. "Okay. You can be on my crew. You're the only person who's ever handed me the right pliers."
success.art: A woman in a stage headset climbing down a ladder and taking a pair of pliers from a teenager in a cluttered projection booth

failure.text: You hand her the wrong wire. There is a pop, a shower of sparks, and every light in the Glitter Box goes out. In the dark, Frankie sighs. "Tomorrow I'm teaching you color codes. Bring a notebook."
failure.art: A dark projection booth lit only by a falling shower of sparks, a woman on a ladder silhouetted against the flash

choices.label: Search the reel for the spliced-in frame

success.text: You find it under the loupe: a single hand-painted frame of the Heartstone, glowing, with a crowd of tiny people around it all looking up. Frankie leans in close. "That's the roundabout on Crystal Street. Somebody wants us to see that." She hands you a spare headset. "Welcome to the crew."
success.art: A teenager peering through a magnifying loupe at a strip of film held up to a lamp, one tiny picture glowing purple with a tiny painted geode

failure.text: You hold the frame up to the lamp and it starts to bubble and burn, the way film does when a projector jams. For one second, in the browning celluloid, you see your own face. Frankie pulls it away. "Okay, enough for today. Tomorrow."
failure.art: A strip of film curling and burning in front of a hot lamp, a teenager's face briefly visible in the melting celluloid

choices.label: Climb to the catwalk and free the stuck sandbag

success.text: You shimmy out onto the catwalk, wrestle the jammed counterweight free and lower it hand over hand. Frankie whistles through the headset. "That's been stuck since Easter. Anybody who'll climb my catwalk is on my team."
success.art: A teenager balanced on a narrow theatre catwalk hauling on a rope line, a sandbag swinging below, a woman in a headset cheering from the stage

failure.text: The sandbag slips and drops, missing Glory by a single sequin. Glory does not scream. Glory hits a high C that cracks a mirror. Frankie gets you down safely and very firmly out. "You're banned until tomorrow. Then you're trained."
failure.art: A heavy sandbag thudding onto a stage inches from a startled drag queen in sequins, a teenager clinging to the catwalk above

name: Pearl Washington
role: Porch sentinel and retired Army radio operator
bio: Pearl Washington ran a radio set for the Women's Army Corps in 1944, came home, married Harold, and in 1959 the two of them became one of the first Black families on Crystal Street after a fight with the developer that she still describes in detail. Harold has been gone eight years. Pearl has not missed a sunset on her porch since. She keeps a logbook of every strange thing the Heartstone has ever done, a double-barrel shotgun loaded with rock salt across her knees, and a story for every house on the street. She is sharp, funny, proud, and stubborn as a mule; she refuses to see a doctor, talks to Harold out loud, and has never once been wrong about a ghost.

perk.name: Rock Salt and Scripture
perk.text: Pearl has been salting ghosts since Truman: +2 on every roll against paranormal nightmares.

meet.title: The Logbook
meet.place: Pearl Washington's porch, Crystal Street
meet.text: Mrs. Washington's porch faces the roundabout and the Heartstone in it like a front-row seat. She is in her rocker with an Army field radio in pieces on a TV tray and a logbook open on her knee, every page dated back to 1959. "Stone's humming early this year," she says without looking up. "Three days early. Sit, if you're going to sit. Help, if you're going to help. Don't stand there like a mailbox."
meet.art: An elderly woman in a marigold headwrap and Army field jacket rocking on a suburban porch, a disassembled field radio on a TV tray, a logbook on her knee, a purple geode glowing in the roundabout beyond

choices.label: Sit on the step and hear her ghost story all the way through

success.text: She tells you about the quarry collapse of 1952, and the singing that came up through the water that night. You don't interrupt once. When she's done she presses a coffee can of rock salt into your hands. "You listen. Most people don't. You come by every evening now, hear?"
success.art: A teenager sitting on porch steps listening to an elderly woman in a rocker, a coffee can of rock salt between them, dusk light turning purple

failure.text: You check your watch twice. She notices both times. "Come back when you've got patience," she says, and closes the logbook. Behind you, the Heartstone pulses once, brighter, as if it was listening too.
failure.art: An elderly woman closing a logbook with a disapproving look, a teenager glancing back at a giant geode glowing brighter in the roundabout

choices.label: Help her put the old field radio back together

success.text: You find the cracked tube and swap in a spare. The set warms up with a hum, and through the static comes a voice on a frequency nobody should be using, counting backward from seven. Pearl writes it down. "Well, soldier, looks like you're on my watch now."
success.art: A vintage Army field radio glowing to life on a TV tray, an elderly woman writing in a logbook, a teenager holding a vacuum tube

failure.text: The radio crackles to life with a child's laughter, far away and underwater. Pearl reaches over and switches it off without a word. "Not today," she says. "Come back tomorrow. I'll have it tuned somewhere friendlier."
failure.art: An elderly woman switching off a crackling vintage radio, her hand trembling slightly, ripples of static drawn in the air

choices.label: Volunteer to walk her salt line around the roundabout

success.text: You pour the line around the Heartstone in one steady circle while the stone hums at your back. You don't look at it. Pearl nods from her porch, the way a sergeant nods. "Steady hands. You'll do. You're with me."
success.art: A teenager pouring a careful circle of white rock salt around a giant glowing purple geode, an elderly woman watching approvingly from her porch

failure.text: A wind comes out of nowhere and blows your salt into the shape of a hand reaching for her house. Pearl sweeps it away with her slipper. "Tomorrow," she says. "And you walk it clockwise."
failure.art: Spilled rock salt on a suburban lawn shaped like a reaching hand, an elderly woman sweeping it away with a pink slipper

name: Bea Lindqvist
bio: Bea Lindqvist skipped second and fourth grade, won the county science fair with a ghost detector built out of a Speak and Learn and a toaster, and is currently on Volume 4 of her notebook, MONSTER FACTS. Her parents are both dentists who are very busy; her teenage brothers pretend she does not exist. She lives next door, runs a treehouse lab with a periscope and a rope ladder she controls, and talks to everyone on channel nine. Bea is brilliant, bossy, fearless in the way only an eleven-year-old can be, and absolutely not going home. Her flaw is that she would rather be wrong alone than right with help, and she gets very small and quiet when someone calls her cute.

perk.name: Monster Facts Vol. 4
perk.text: Bea has cross-referenced everything: the case board shows your odds of finding each clue.

meet.title: The Treehouse Lab
meet.place: The Lindqvists' backyard treehouse, Crystal Street
meet.text: The treehouse next door has a periscope, a NO ADULTS sign and a rope ladder that is currently pulled up. A walkie-talkie dangles on a string in front of your face. It crackles. "State your name and your business. Over." Above you, a small girl in giant red glasses is aiming a homemade meter made from a colander at the Heartstone. "Also, I'm conducting science, so be quick. Over."
meet.art: A backyard treehouse with a periscope and a hand-painted kids-only sign, a small blonde girl in red glasses aiming a colander contraption at a glowing geode, a walkie-talkie dangling on a string

choices.label: Take her monster-facts entrance exam

success.text: "What do you put across a doorway to stop a ghost?" Salt. "What do vampires count?" Spilled seeds. "Wrong, they count anything, but I'll allow it." The ladder drops. She clips a walkie-talkie to your belt. "Channel nine. You're in. Over."
success.art: A rope ladder dropping from a treehouse, a small girl in red glasses holding out a walkie-talkie to a teenager climbing up

failure.text: You say vampires hate garlic bread. "WRONG," she announces, and the walkie goes silent. A paper airplane floats down with a study guide drawn on it in crayon. "Retake tomorrow. Over and out."
failure.art: A paper airplane covered in crayon diagrams of monsters floating down from a treehouse to a teenager below

choices.label: Climb up and help calibrate her Heartstone meter

success.text: You realize the colander is picking up the radio tower, adjust it, and the needle swings straight at the Heartstone and pins. Bea gasps. "It gets stronger at dusk. I've been wrong for a week and you fixed it in a minute. You're my lab partner now. Don't let it go to your head."
success.art: A teenager and a small girl in red glasses inside a treehouse lab, a homemade meter's needle pinned toward a glowing geode outside the window

failure.text: The meter makes a noise like a cat and explodes into a confetti of aluminum foil. Mrs. Lindqvist calls Bea in for lunch. Bea, covered in foil, does not go. "Tomorrow," she tells you darkly. "Bring better wire."
failure.art: A small girl in red glasses covered in shreds of aluminum foil in a treehouse, a smoking colander contraption, a mother calling from the back porch

choices.label: Promise she can come on every stakeout

success.text: She studies your face like a microscope slide. Then she spits in her palm and holds it out. You shake. "Binding contract," Bea says. "Also I'm in charge of the notebook. Over."
success.art: A small girl in red glasses solemnly shaking a teenager's hand from a treehouse doorway, a notebook tucked under her arm

failure.text: "You're just humoring me. Everybody humors me." The walkie clicks off. The periscope swivels away from you. You will have to prove it tomorrow.
failure.art: A treehouse periscope swiveling away from a teenager standing alone in a backyard, a silent walkie-talkie on a string

name: Jesse "Moose" Kowalski
bio: Jesse Kowalski is six-foot-five, two hundred sixty pounds, and the reason half the Glimmer Falls varsity squad wears matching crimson scarves: he knits them on the bench between series, a habit his babcia taught him to keep his hands from shaking. He is bi, out to his sister and his best friend, went to homecoming with a girl last year, and has spent this whole fall working up the courage to say hi to a boy in the marching band's drumline. Moose is gentle, goofy, and the first person to step between a smaller kid and trouble. His flaw is that he swallows every conflict until it boils over, can't say no to anyone, and worries about everybody except himself.

perk.name: Big Guy Block
perk.text: Moose plants himself between you and whatever's coming: once per night, cancel the nerve loss from one failed roll.

meet.title: Between Sets
meet.place: The roller-rink annex, Pump Iron Gym and Aerobics
meet.text: In the corner of Pump Iron, where the weight room spills into the old roller-rink annex, the biggest teenager you have ever seen is spotting a nervous freshman on the bench press with one hand and knitting a crimson scarf with the other. Two seniors in tank tops are snickering at the needles. "Hey Grandma, knit me a cardigan." Moose's ears go red, but he just keeps counting reps out loud, gently, for the freshman.
meet.art: A giant teenage boy in a letter jacket spotting a skinny freshman on a bench press while holding knitting needles, two smirking seniors in tank tops nearby, an old roller rink visible through an archway

choices.label: Sit down and ask him to teach you to knit

success.text: He lights up like a scoreboard. Knit two, purl two, and by the end of the set you've got four lumpy rows. The seniors drift away, bored. Moose bumps your shoulder with his. "You're a natural. Stick with me, okay? I mean it. I've got your back."
success.art: A huge teenage boy patiently guiding a teenager's hands on knitting needles on a gym bench, crimson yarn trailing between them

failure.text: The yarn knots into something that looks like a spiderweb and then like a spider. Moose laughs his big honking laugh, not at you. "Come back tomorrow. I'll cast on for you first. Everybody's first scarf is a monster."
failure.art: A tangled knot of crimson yarn in a teenager's lap shaped vaguely like a spider, a huge boy laughing kindly beside them

choices.label: Offer to spot him on his own heavy set

success.text: Moose loads the bar to a number you don't want to think about. You hold your breath and your grip, and on the last rep you help him rack it with a clang. He sits up beaming. "Nobody ever offers to spot me. They figure I don't need it. You're my guy now."
success.art: A teenager straining to help rack a heavy barbell over a giant boy on a bench, both grinning, plates clanging

failure.text: The bar dips toward his chest and he catches it himself, with one arm, gently, so you don't feel bad. "Maybe warm up first tomorrow," he says, rubbing your shoulder. "I'll be here. I'm always here."
failure.art: A giant teenage boy pressing a sagging barbell back up one-handed while a teenager winces above him

choices.label: Tell the seniors to knock it off

success.text: "Hey. His scarves keep your whole team warm. What have you made lately, besides noise?" The seniors mutter and leave. Moose stares at you. Then he wraps the half-finished scarf around your neck. "That's yours when it's done. You and me, okay?"
success.art: A teenager facing down two seniors in a gym, a huge boy behind them looping a half-finished crimson scarf around the teenager's neck

failure.text: They laugh you off like a mosquito. Moose stands up, all six-foot-five of him, and they leave fast, but you feel about two inches tall. He catches up at the door. "Thanks for trying. Really. Come back tomorrow?"
failure.art: Two seniors backing away from a towering teenage boy, a smaller teenager standing at the gym door looking deflated

name: Priya Raman
bio: Priya Raman is captain of the Glimmer Falls mathletes, a state finalist in two events, and on Friday nights the dungeon master of The Crystal Kingdoms, a homebrew campaign she has run in the library meeting room since seventh grade. Her parents expect pre-med; she wants to write game modules for a living and has three binders of graph-paper dungeons to prove it. This fall her notes have started coming true: the lich she invented, the drowned counselor, the house that eats guests. Priya is precise, competitive, a total rules lawyer and a secret softie for her players. Her flaw is perfectionism, and the fear, which she tells no one, that she imagined all of this into being.

perk.name: DM's Mercy
perk.text: Priya rules that one didn't count: reroll one failed roll each night.

meet.title: Session Zero
meet.place: The meeting room, Glimmer Falls Public Library
meet.text: The library meeting room is set for six players, with character sheets, snacks and a cardboard DM screen. Only one chair is full. Priya Raman sits behind the screen, staring at a map she drew in August: a cul-de-sac, a roundabout, a glowing stone, and in her neat handwriting, HERE THE SLEEPERS LOSE THEIR COLOR. "My players quit," she says. "Everything I wrote for them started happening. You can sit down, I guess. Everyone else is scared of my campaign."
meet.art: A library meeting room table set for a tabletop game with empty chairs and character sheets, a girl in a purple cardigan behind a cardboard game screen staring at a hand-drawn map of a cul-de-sac

choices.label: Roll up a character and play her one-player campaign

success.text: You roll a bard named Sir Vical and seduce a gelatinous cube with a sea shanty. Priya tries to keep a straight face, fails, and laughs so hard she snorts. "That's not in the rules. That's BETTER than the rules." She slides a character sheet over with your name on it. "Party of two. For real."
success.art: A teenager and a girl in a purple cardigan laughing over a tabletop game, dice scattered across a hand-drawn map, a cardboard game screen between them

failure.text: Your bard dies in round one to a ceiling mimic. At the exact moment Priya says the word ceiling, the real ceiling tile above you creaks. You both look up. Priya packs up very fast. "Session's over. Reroll tomorrow."
failure.art: Two teenagers frozen at a game table staring up at a creaking library ceiling tile, dice scattered, a character sheet with a skull drawn on it

choices.label: Compare her dungeon maps against a real town map

success.text: You lay a Glimmer Falls street map over her dungeon. The tunnels line up exactly with the storm drains under Crystal Street. Priya stares. "So I'm not causing it. I'm picking it up. Like a radio." She closes the binder. "I need a co-DM. You're hired."
success.art: A town street map and a hand-drawn dungeon map overlaid on a light table, tunnels aligning with storm drains, two teenagers leaning over them

failure.text: When you lay the maps together, the ink on hers starts to run, crawling across the paper toward the roundabout like it's late for something. Priya snatches it away. "Okay. Tomorrow. I need to think about this. Alone. No, not alone. Tomorrow."
failure.art: Black ink crawling across a hand-drawn map toward a drawn roundabout, a girl snatching the paper off a library table

choices.label: Convince her that her notes are a warning, not a curse

success.text: You tell her about the Heartstone: how it amplifies what people feel. "You didn't make the monsters. You just listen better than anyone else in this town." Priya's eyes are wet behind her glasses. She hands you the gold die. "Hold onto that. You're in my party."
success.art: A girl in a purple cardigan pressing a gold twenty-sided die into a teenager's palm across a game table, both of them smiling

failure.text: She shakes her head. "That's what a DM says to make the players feel better." She closes the screen, and for a second you see her map's roundabout glow through the cardboard. "Come back tomorrow. Maybe I'll believe you then."
failure.art: A girl closing a cardboard game screen, a faint purple glow leaking through it from the map beneath

name: Lou "Lightning" Tran
bio: Lou Tran holds the high score on every cabinet at Starlight Arcade except one, and that one is killing him. His parents run the Saigon Noodle stand in the food court, and between homework and refills he has turned their dinner rush into a training regimen; he can catch a falling chopstick without looking. He keeps a coin belt of quarters for every emergency and a coffee can at home where he is saving to buy his mom a dishwasher. Lou is cocky, hilarious and an absolute menace at trash talk. His flaw is that he hates losing more than he loves winning, can't sit still for more than a minute, and hides how much he worries his family is working too hard for him.

perk.name: Extra Life
perk.text: Lou always has one more continue: reroll one failed roll each night.

meet.title: Nightmare Lane
meet.place: Starlight Arcade, Starlight Mall
meet.text: In the back of Starlight Arcade there is a cabinet nobody remembers being delivered. It's called NIGHTMARE LANE, the art on the side is a suburban street at night, and the top score has belonged to the same initials since it arrived: FKR. A kid with a lightning bolt shaved into his hair is pounding the buttons, loses, and kicks the coin door. "Every machine in this place says LOU at the top," he says. "Except this one. You any good?"
meet.art: A shadowy arcade cabinet in the back of a neon arcade, side art of a suburban street at night, a high score screen with three mysterious initials, a boy with a lightning bolt haircut glaring at it

choices.label: Challenge him to one round on his favorite machine

success.text: You lose. Obviously. But you lose by only forty thousand points, which nobody ever has. Lou stares at the screen, then at you. "Okay, you got hands. You're my player two." He flips you a quarter from his belt. "Keep it. Emergencies."
success.art: Two teenagers side by side at a glowing arcade cabinet, one grinning and flipping a quarter to the other, scores flashing on screen

failure.text: Game over in twenty-eight seconds. Lou winces like he's watching a car crash. "Okay. Okay. That was... a learning experience. Come back tomorrow, I'll teach you the pattern." He's already putting another quarter in.
failure.art: A GAME OVER screen glowing red on an arcade cabinet, a boy with a lightning bolt haircut wincing beside a slumped teenager

choices.label: Take on NIGHTMARE LANE together, one hand each

success.text: You take the joystick, he takes the buttons. On the last level the screen shows a pink salon chair and a figure with shears, and you don't flinch. The score rolls past FKR's. The initials flicker and vanish. Lou is speechless for the first time in recorded history. "We're a team now. That's not up for discussion."
success.art: Two teenagers sharing the controls of an arcade cabinet, the screen showing a pixelated salon chair and a shadowy figure with shears, the old initials dissolving

failure.text: The cabinet eats your quarter, then spits it back out wrapped in a single long gray hair. The screen flashes NEXT APPOINTMENT: SOON. Lou unplugs the machine. It keeps glowing. "Tomorrow," he says, "we bring backup."
failure.art: A quarter wrapped in a long gray hair sitting in an arcade coin return, the unplugged cabinet still glowing with a sinister message

choices.label: Help his mom through the dinner rush at the noodle stand

success.text: You bus trays, refill sriracha and charm a table of mall walkers into ordering extra spring rolls. Mrs. Tran gives you a bowl on the house. Lou, slurping beside you, says, "Mom likes you more than me now. You have to be on my crew so I can keep an eye on you."
success.art: A busy food court noodle stand, a teenager carrying a tray of steaming bowls, a boy with a lightning bolt haircut grinning, a smiling woman behind the counter

failure.text: You drop a full tray of pho in front of a mall security guard. Mrs. Tran is very nice about it, which is worse. Lou pats your back. "Tomorrow you just do napkins. Napkins can't spill."
failure.art: Spilled noodle soup across a food court floor, a teenager frozen in horror, a boy patting their back

name: Father Ignatius "Iggy" Reyes
bio: Father Iggy Reyes grew up in Daly City, played bass in garage bands through seminary, and was sent to St. Jude's in Glimmer Falls as the young priest who would 'connect with the youth.' He did not expect the youth to show up with squirt guns asking him to bless them, and he did not expect to say yes every time. His band, the Venial Sins, practices in the church basement on Thursdays; his youth group is the only one in the county where queer kids are welcomed by name. His lola told him stories about aswang, and he took notes. Iggy is warm, irreverent and a little too eager to be the cool priest; he can't keep time on bass, feuds with the monsignor, and carries guilt for a friend he couldn't help.

perk.name: Blessed Squirt Gun
perk.text: Iggy blessed the whole arsenal and didn't ask a single question: +2 on every roll against cult nightmares.

meet.title: Thursday Practice
meet.place: The basement of St. Jude's
meet.text: The basement of St. Jude's smells like coffee urns and amplifier dust. A priest with a black spiked pompadour is tuning a red bass under a felt banner that says GOD IS LOVE in glitter glue, while the stone holy-water font in the corner bubbles like a pot left on the stove. "That's been doing that since Monday," Father Iggy says cheerfully. "I'm choosing to treat it as a sign. Are you here for youth group, band practice, or the other thing?" He nods at a bucket of neon squirt guns.
meet.art: A church basement with folding chairs and a felt banner, a priest with a spiked pompadour tuning a red electric bass, a stone holy-water font bubbling in the corner, a bucket of neon squirt guns

choices.label: Pick up a tambourine and jam with the Venial Sins

success.text: The Venial Sins blast through a three-chord version of a hymn, and you nail every tambourine hit. Iggy does a knee slide across the linoleum. "Okay, you're in the band. And you're in the other thing. Mostly the other thing."
success.art: A priest in a leather jacket doing a knee slide with a red bass across a church basement floor, a teenager shaking a tambourine, amps glowing

failure.text: The feedback shrieks through the amp and every candle in the basement goes out at once. In the dark, Iggy says, "That was either the amp or a very strong review. Come back tomorrow, we'll try it acoustic."
failure.art: A dark church basement lit only by a glowing amplifier, every candle extinguished with smoke curling up, band members frozen mid-song

choices.label: Hand him a squirt gun and ask for a blessing, no questions

success.text: He doesn't ask a single question. He fills it from the bubbling font, says a short prayer in Latin and a shorter one in Tagalog, and hands it back with a vial for backup. "Whatever you're fighting, you're not fighting it alone. I'm coming with you."
success.art: A priest filling a neon squirt gun from a bubbling stone font, a teenager holding out their hands, candle light glowing on the water

failure.text: The moment he dips the squirt gun, the font hisses and the water turns black as ink for a heartbeat before clearing. Iggy stares at it. "Okay. I need to call somebody. Come back tomorrow, and maybe stay out of the cemetery tonight."
failure.art: A stone holy-water font with dark ink-black water swirling, a priest pulling back a neon squirt gun with a startled look

choices.label: Go with him to check the founders' graves where kids heard singing

success.text: In Pinecrest, behind the founders' obelisk, the grass is pressed down in a perfect circle, and someone has left a ring of dried herbs. You don't run. Iggy squeezes your shoulder. "Most people would've bolted. I want you with me for whatever this is."
success.art: A teenager and a priest in a leather jacket standing at the edge of a circle of flattened grass in an old cemetery, a ring of dried herbs, a stone obelisk behind them

failure.text: A sound comes from inside the founders' crypt, like many people humming one note through closed lips. You're back at the church before you remember running. Iggy is right behind you. "Tomorrow," he pants. "In daylight. With the band."
failure.art: A teenager and a priest sprinting down a cemetery path away from a dark crypt, gravestones blurred, a faint glow behind the crypt door

name: Sunny Castellanos
bio: Sunny Castellanos grew up in the Bronx, moved west with her abuela at sixteen, and has been the fastest person in Glimmer Falls on any surface ever since: track, parking lot, roller rink, or the hill down Crystal Street she is not allowed to race anymore. She has used a wheelchair since a spinal injury at nine and built her racing chair with Joey Benally's help. She is training for the 1988 Paralympics in Seoul and teaches a 6 a.m. class at Pump Iron that is pure joy: salsa, sweat and shouting. Sunny is loud, funny, competitive and generous. Her flaws are impatience and pride; she hates being helped without being asked and can't stand being called inspiring by people who won't race her.

perk.name: Sunrise Warm-up
perk.text: Sunny drags the whole crew through her dawn class whether they like it or not: +1 nerve each dawn.

meet.title: Empty Class
meet.place: The aerobics studio, Pump Iron Gym and Aerobics
meet.text: Sunny Castellanos's 4 p.m. aerobics class usually has twenty people in it. Today it has a boom box, a mirrored wall and Sunny, in an orange headband, glaring at a VHS box someone left on the bench: VONDA VELOUR'S BURN TO THE BONE. "They all bought this tape," she says. "They say they can't stop doing it. They say it's fun." She spins her chair to face you. "You. You want to sweat or you want to talk?"
meet.art: An empty mirrored aerobics studio with a boom box on the floor, a woman in an orange headband in a sleek racing wheelchair glaring at a lurid aerobics videotape on a bench

choices.label: Lace up rink skates and race her around the roller annex

success.text: She laps you twice. You never stop skating. When you finally cross the line, Sunny is waiting with a towel and a grin. "You're slow, but you don't quit. I can work with that. You're with me."
success.art: A woman in a racing wheelchair lapping a wobbling teenager on roller skates around an old roller rink, colored lights spinning overhead

failure.text: You wipe out on the first turn, spectacularly, into a stack of rental skates. Sunny circles back, offers a hand and waits until you take it. "Tomorrow we start with braking. Braking is not optional."
failure.art: A teenager sprawled in a pile of rental roller skates, a woman in a racing wheelchair holding out a gloved hand

choices.label: Do her entire class, start to finish, just the two of you

success.text: Forty minutes of salsa, punches and shouting, and you do not stop. At the end you're both laughing and dripping. Sunny pops the Vonda tape out of its box and drops it in the trash. "That's what exercise is supposed to feel like. Joy. You're on my crew."
success.art: A teenager and a woman in a racing wheelchair laughing and drenched in sweat in a mirrored studio, a videotape tossed into a trash can

failure.text: You make it eleven minutes before you lie down on the floor and become one with the carpet. Sunny rolls over with a cup of water. "Not bad for a first day. Come back tomorrow. I'll go easy. I won't go easy."
failure.art: A teenager collapsed flat on an aerobics studio floor, a woman in a wheelchair holding out a paper cup of water, boom box still playing

choices.label: Ask what exactly her students said about the tape

success.text: She tells you: they do the tape at midnight, every midnight, and the woman on the screen counts them down and won't let them stop. "Mrs. Delgado's seventy. She cried in the parking lot." Sunny cracks her knuckles. "I'm not losing my people to a tape. You in?"
success.art: A woman in a racing wheelchair holding up a lurid aerobics videotape, her face serious, a teenager listening in a mirrored studio

failure.text: "Don't look at me like that. I don't need a pep talk." She thinks you're pitying her, and her chair is already turning away. "Come back when you want to sweat, not talk." The VHS box on the bench seems to smile.
failure.art: A woman in a wheelchair turning away from a teenager in an empty studio, a videotape box on a bench with a smiling aerobics star on the cover

name: Wade Whitfield
bio: Wade Whitfield is repeating his senior year, works the crusher at Rusty's Junkyard, and lives about half the time in his black van, which has a wizard airbrushed on the side and a cassette deck that only plays one tape. His dad left when he was ten; he drives his little sister to school every morning and threatens anyone who looks at her funny. Everybody in Glimmer Falls thinks Wade is a burnout. Nobody knows about the spiral notebook in his glove box full of poems about the moon, the quarry and his mom working nights. Wade is loyal to the bone, funnier than people expect, and braver than he should be. His flaws: he hides every soft thing behind noise, procrastinates everything, and drives like a maniac.

perk.name: Glovebox Sonnet
perk.text: Every morning Wade reads the crew one poem from the notebook and dares anyone to laugh: +1 nerve each dawn.

meet.title: The Van Won't Start
meet.place: The back lot, Rusty's Junkyard
meet.text: In the back lot of Rusty's, a black van with a wizard airbrushed on the side is making a noise like a dying cow. A guy with a feathered mullet is kicking the tire and swearing creatively. When he yanks open the glove box for a wrench, a spiral notebook falls out at your feet and flops open. The page says, in careful pencil: the quarry keeps the moon like a coin / nobody in this town ever spends. Wade freezes. "That's... my sister's."
meet.art: A black van with an airbrushed wizard on the side in a junkyard, a guy with a feathered mullet frozen mid-kick, a spiral notebook lying open on the gravel at a teenager's feet

choices.label: Hand back the notebook and tell him the poem is good

success.text: "The coin line is really good," you say, and you mean it. Wade turns brick red. Then he grins, slowly, like a sunrise. "Nobody's ever read one. Okay. Okay, you're cool. You're riding with me from now on."
success.art: A guy with a mullet taking a spiral notebook from a teenager, blushing and grinning, the black van behind them in golden afternoon light

failure.text: You mean to say it's good, but you snort a little at the word 'moon' and he snatches the notebook back. "Whatever. It's my sister's." He's not mad, exactly; he's embarrassed. "Come back tomorrow. I'll... think about it."
failure.art: A guy with a mullet shoving a spiral notebook into his vest, avoiding eye contact, a teenager wincing beside a black van

choices.label: Help him push-start the van down the junk hill

success.text: You both shove, the van rolls, Wade pops the clutch and the engine roars to life with a blast of heavy metal from the tape deck. He leans out the window, hand up for a high five. "Get in, slowpoke. You're crew now."
success.art: A black van roaring down a gravel hill in a junkyard, a guy with a mullet leaning out the window for a high five, a teenager running alongside

failure.text: The van rolls, does not start, and keeps rolling, straight into the car maze. It takes an hour to find it again, wedged between a hearse and an ice cream truck. Wade sighs. "Tomorrow. With Joey. Joey knows vans."
failure.art: A black van wedged between a hearse and an ice cream truck deep in a junkyard car maze, two figures staring at it in dismay

choices.label: Fix the jammed cassette deck while he works on the engine

success.text: You unspool the tape with a pencil, and when the deck clicks back to life the whole junkyard echoes with a guitar solo. Somewhere in the car maze, every stray dog howls along. Wade nods slowly. "Respect. You get to pick the tape. Sometimes. You're in."
success.art: A teenager in the passenger seat of a van fixing a cassette deck with a pencil, a guy with a mullet nodding in approval, dogs howling in the distance

failure.text: The tape snaps. It was the only tape. Wade stares at the two shiny ends for a long moment. "That was my dad's." He breathes out. "It's okay. It's okay. Come back tomorrow, man, I need a minute."
failure.art: A guy with a mullet holding a snapped cassette tape in both hands, two loose ends of tape fluttering, the van door hanging open

name: Zelda Fishbein
role: Former scream queen, video store clerk
bio: From 1951 to 1959 Zelda Fishbein screamed her way through eleven pictures, including Brides of the Atom and The Thing from Crystal Springs, and walked away from the movies when the studio wanted her to become Zelda Fisher and fix her nose. She kept her name and her nose. Now she works the counter at Rewind Video, judges your rentals out loud, and lives in a little house by the creek with Ruth, her 'roommate' of thirty years, who makes the best rugelach in the county. Zelda knows exactly how every monster movie ends, and why. She is tough, nosy, hilarious and sentimental; her flaw is that she spoils every ending, never lets anyone take care of her, and still quietly mourns the scream they kept and the name they cut.

perk.name: Final Girl Rules
perk.text: Zelda has outlived forty movie slashers and taught you every rule: +2 on every roll against slasher nightmares.

meet.title: The Night-Drop Slot
meet.place: The counter, Rewind Video
meet.text: Behind the counter at Rewind Video, under a poster for a 1954 picture called Brides of the Atom, a woman with a silver-streaked bouffant is eyeing the night-drop slot. It has been growling since yesterday. "Every morning there's a tape in there that nobody rented," Zelda Fishbein says, "and every tape has a new ending." She looks at your hands. "Before you ask, no, you can't rent the adults-only aisle. And yes, I'm going to judge whatever you pick."
meet.art: A cluttered video store counter beneath an old painted monster movie advertisement, a woman in a silver-streaked bouffant and cat-eye glasses eyeing a metal night-drop slot in the wall that seems to be growling

choices.label: Take her challenge and name how a classic monster movie ends

success.text: "The scientist's daughter climbs the tower and talks to it. Nobody shoots." Zelda takes off her glasses. "Nobody your age knows that one. I was the daughter." She slides an employee discount card across the counter. "You're with me now, kiddo."
success.art: A woman in cat-eye glasses sliding a card across a video store counter to a teenager, an old black-and-white movie still on the wall behind her

failure.text: You guess wrong. Zelda clutches her pearls like you've insulted her mother. She hands you a tape with a sticky note: WATCH THIS. THEN COME BACK. "Tomorrow. And you rewind it before you return it."
failure.art: A woman in a bouffant handing a teenager a VHS tape with a sticky note on it across a counter, a disappointed look on her face

choices.label: Ask about the poster and the pictures she made

success.text: Her whole face lights up. Twenty minutes later you know about the rubber atom suit, the director who drank, and the scream she recorded once and heard in forty movies after. "Nobody asks anymore." She pats your hand. "Come by any time. I mean it. I'll come by too, if there's trouble."
success.art: A woman in cat-eye glasses telling a story with big hand gestures across a video store counter, a teenager laughing, an old painted movie advertisement above them

failure.text: "I don't sign autographs for gawkers," she says, and turns away to sort returns. Then, more softly: "Sorry, kid. Bad morning. Come back tomorrow and ask me again."
failure.art: A woman in a bouffant turning away to sort a stack of videotapes, a teenager standing awkwardly at the counter

choices.label: Reach into the growling night-drop slot for today's tape

success.text: Your arm goes in up to the elbow and comes out with a warm tape labeled with tomorrow's date. Zelda puts it in the counter VCR. It shows the Heartstone at night with a crowd around it. She ejects it, grim. "Final girls don't go it alone. Neither do I. I'm coming with you."
success.art: A teenager pulling a VHS tape out of a metal night-drop slot, a woman in cat-eye glasses watching a small counter TV showing a glowing geode at night

failure.text: The slot snaps shut on your fingers like a mouth. When you yank free, there's a perfect ring of tiny teeth marks on your knuckles. Zelda hands you a bandage. "Rule six: don't put your hand in anything. Come back tomorrow."
failure.art: A metal night-drop slot snapping shut, a teenager clutching their hand, a woman in cat-eye glasses holding out a bandage

name: Kevin "Kev" Park
role: Paperboy with a map of every secret
bio: Kevin Park throws the Glimmer Falls Gazette onto ninety-one porches every morning by 6 a.m. from a red BMX with playing cards clothespinned to the spokes. His parents run Park's Cleaners on Main, so he also knows whose suits came in with mud on the cuffs. He knows which dogs bite, which porch lights stay on all night, who gets weird mail, and that nobody, ever, delivers to number 13. Kev considers himself a businessman, not a kid, and sells information for candy at reasonable rates. He is fast, funny, endlessly curious and braver on a bike than on foot. His flaw is that he cannot keep a secret to save his life, and he talks fastest when he is scared.

perk.name: Paper Route Tips
perk.text: Kev splits his tips with his business partners, as is only fair: +2 quarters each dawn.

meet.title: Number Thirteen
meet.place: The end of the cul-de-sac, Crystal Street
meet.text: A red BMX is lying on its side at the curb in front of 13 Crystal Street, the model home nobody ever bought. Its owner, a skinny kid in a backwards cap, is standing as far from the lawn as physics allows. Half his newspapers have blown across the perfect grass to the perfect porch. "I don't go on that lawn," Kev Park says. "Nobody goes on that lawn. Mr. Pruitt's dog went on that lawn in 1984 and now it only barks backward."
meet.art: A red BMX lying at the curb in front of an immaculate, too-perfect model home, newspapers scattered across its flawless lawn, a skinny boy in a backwards cap standing well back on the sidewalk

choices.label: Walk onto the lawn at 13 and gather his papers

success.text: The grass is soft as carpet and the front curtains twitch, but you gather every paper and walk, not run, back to the curb. Kev stares at you like you just landed on the moon. "You're my business partner now. Fifty-fifty. Okay, sixty-forty. Okay, fifty-fifty."
success.art: A teenager walking calmly off a perfect lawn with an armful of newspapers, curtains twitching in the model home behind them, a boy on the sidewalk gaping

failure.text: You reach the third paper and the sprinklers come on with a hiss like a breath. The front door clicks open an inch. You run. Kev is already halfway down the street. "Come back tomorrow!" he yells over his shoulder. "From a DISTANCE!"
failure.art: A teenager fleeing across a perfect lawn as sprinklers hiss on and the front door of a model home creaks open, a boy on a BMX pedaling away

choices.label: Offer him a deal: help with the route for one good secret

success.text: You finish his route together in record time. As promised, he leans in close. "Number 7. The new family. Their lights come on all at the same second every night, every room. Like one guy flips one switch." He shakes your hand like a banker. "Pleasure doing business. Partners."
success.art: A boy on a BMX and a teenager on foot tossing newspapers onto suburban porches, the boy leaning in to whisper, a pristine house glowing in the background

failure.text: Kev is a better negotiator than you. By the end of the route you have somehow paid him a quarter for the privilege of helping him. "Come back tomorrow," he says brightly. "I'll give you the friends-and-family rate."
failure.art: A grinning boy on a BMX pocketing a quarter from a bewildered teenager on a suburban sidewalk at dawn

choices.label: Race him to finish the rest of the route before 6 a.m.

success.text: You sprint, he pedals, and every paper lands on the right porch at 5:58. Kev skids to a stop, breathless and delighted. "Nobody's ever kept up with me. You're hired. You're crew. You're both."
success.art: A boy on a red BMX and a teenager running side by side down a suburban street at dawn, newspapers flying onto porches

failure.text: You throw a paper through Mrs. Abernathy's screen door. She comes out in curlers. Kev pedals away so fast his playing cards scream. You get the lecture alone. Tomorrow, he'll owe you one.
failure.art: An angry woman in curlers and a bathrobe holding a newspaper at a torn screen door, a teenager standing guilty on the porch, a BMX speeding away

name: Raven
bio: Raven reads tarot for a quarter on the steps of the Ashworth mausoleum in Pinecrest Cemetery, dresses entirely in velvet from the St. Jude's rummage sale, and knows the name and story on every grave older than 1900. In 1986 there aren't many words for someone who is neither a boy nor a girl, so Raven just says, "Call me Raven, no pronoun needed," and waits to see who listens; the crew learns to say they, and it means more to Raven than they will ever admit. They are dry, dramatic, aloof until they decide you are worth it, and secretly obsessed with cheesy creature features and cartoon bears. Their flaw is that they test everyone before they trust them, and they would rather tell your fortune than talk about their own.

perk.name: The Spread
perk.text: Raven lays out the cards each morning and reads where the truth is hiding: the case board shows your odds of finding each clue.

meet.title: The Tower
meet.place: The Ashworth mausoleum, Pinecrest Cemetery
meet.text: On the steps of the oldest mausoleum in Pinecrest sits someone in plum velvet with a deck of tarot cards and a hand-lettered sign: FORTUNES 25 CENTS, TRUTH EXTRA. A crow on the roof watches you. They flip a card before you even sit down: a tower struck by lightning. "Huh," they say. "That's yours. That's bad." When you ask their name, they say, "Raven. No pronoun needed." Then they wait, the way people wait who have been disappointed before.
meet.art: A goth teen in a plum velvet frock coat sitting on the steps of an old stone mausoleum with a tarot spread, a hand-lettered cardboard sign, a crow perched on the roof above

choices.label: Pay your quarter and let them finish the reading

success.text: Tower, then the Star, then the Six of Cups. "Something falls," Raven says, "and then you get help from people you didn't expect. Kids. Old friends." They study you. "The cards say I'm one of them. I hate when the cards are right." They fall in beside you.
success.art: Three tarot cards laid out on a mausoleum step, a teenager and a goth teen in velvet leaning over them, a crow watching from above

failure.text: A cold wind lifts every card off the step and scatters them across the graves. Raven watches them go without moving. "The cards say come back tomorrow," they say. "Also help me find the Hanged Man. He's under a cherub somewhere."
failure.art: Tarot cards blowing across a foggy cemetery between gravestones, a goth teen in velvet watching calmly from a mausoleum step

choices.label: Say their name right and ask how they're doing

success.text: "Nice to meet you, Raven. How are you doing today?" There is a very long pause. The crow caws. Raven looks down at the cards so you don't see their face. "Nobody ever asks the reader." They tuck the Tower back in the deck. "Okay. I'll come with you. Somebody has to keep you alive."
success.art: A goth teen in velvet looking down at a tarot deck to hide a smile, a teenager sitting beside them on the mausoleum steps, a crow cawing above

failure.text: You start the sentence three different ways and trip over every one. Raven rolls their eyes, but not unkindly. "It's a new word for an old thing. Practice. Come back tomorrow and try again." They flip you a card for luck: the Fool.
failure.art: A goth teen in velvet flicking a single tarot card to an embarrassed teenager, a faint smile on their face, mausoleum stones behind them

choices.label: Follow the crow into the founders' row

success.text: The crow leads you to a cracked headstone from 1859 with no name, only a carved sprig of rosemary. Raven kneels and touches it. "Every grave here has a name but this one. Somebody wanted her forgotten." They stand, coat swirling. "Fine. I'm in. We find out who."
success.art: A teenager and a goth teen in velvet kneeling at a weathered unnamed headstone carved with a sprig of rosemary, a crow perched on top, fog curling

failure.text: The crow leads you in a circle and then up onto a stone angel, which turns its head. It definitely turns its head. Raven drags you out the cemetery gate by your sleeve. "New rule: tomorrow, in daylight, and we don't follow birds."
failure.art: A stone cemetery angel with its head turned toward the viewer, a crow on its wing, two teenagers fleeing toward a wrought-iron gate

name: Coach Tammy Jo Pruitt
role: Softball coach and last line of defense
bio: Tammy Jo Pruitt pitched fast-pitch softball for a Tulsa barnstorming team in the sixties, struck out a minor-league home-run king at a county fair, and has coached the Glimmer Falls High Lady Lynx to four league titles. She is six feet tall, built like a refrigerator, and has never lost a fight with a parent, a referee or a monster. Her office door is always open after school, and every kid in town knows it is the safe room: no questions, cold orange slices, a couch. She is loud, blunt, warm under all the gravel and a terrible cook who insists on bringing casseroles anyway. Her flaw is that she would rather run through a wall than talk about a feeling, and she takes every kid's trouble home with her at night.

perk.name: Coach's Got You
perk.text: Tammy Jo steps between you and it, every time: once per night, cancel the nerve loss from one failed roll.

meet.title: Stakeout at the Equipment Shed
meet.place: The softball field, Glimmer Falls High
meet.text: Coach Pruitt is sitting in a lawn chair behind the dugout with a thermos, a pair of binoculars and an aluminum bat across her knees, watching the equipment shed. "Something's been taking my softballs," she says without lowering the binoculars. "Forty-two of 'em. Leaves the door locked and a trail of what I sincerely hope is gravy." She finally looks at you. "You got business here, or you want to make yourself useful?"
meet.art: A tall woman in a green ball cap sitting in a lawn chair behind a dugout with binoculars and a softball bat, a padlocked equipment shed across the field, a trail of brown goo leading to it

choices.label: Grab a helmet and take a few swings off her fastball

success.text: Her first pitch you never see. Her second you foul off. Her third you crack right up the middle and she has to duck. Coach whoops so loud the crows leave. "Now THAT'S a ballplayer. You're on my team. Not the softball team. The other team."
success.art: A teenager in a batting helmet connecting with a softball, a tall coach ducking on the pitcher's mound and laughing, crows scattering

failure.text: Three pitches, three swings, three misses, and you're pretty sure the third one was a changeup out of spite. Coach hands you a helmet with your name taped on it. "Tomorrow, 3:15. We'll fix that swing."
failure.art: A teenager swinging and missing as a softball smacks into a backstop, a coach on the mound shaking her head with a grin

choices.label: Pull up a bucket and join her stakeout

success.text: At four-thirty a cafeteria lunch tray slides out from under the shed door by itself, loaded with softballs, and scoots off toward the school kitchen. You don't scream. Coach writes it on her clipboard. "Kid, you kept your cool. You're with me now. We're following that tray."
success.art: A cafeteria lunch tray loaded with softballs sliding by itself across a ball field, a coach and a teenager crouched behind a dugout watching

failure.text: You doze off on your bucket. When you wake, the shed door is open, your shoelaces are tied together, and there's gravy on your shoes. Coach is furious, at the shed. "Come back tomorrow, and bring coffee."
failure.art: A teenager waking up on an overturned bucket with their shoelaces tied together, an open equipment shed and a trail of gravy, a coach glaring at the shed

choices.label: Tell her straight what has been happening on Crystal Street

success.text: She listens to the whole thing without blinking, then nods once. "I've been coaching for twenty years. When a kid tells me something's wrong, something's wrong." She stands and shoulders the bat. "Okay. Coach is in."
success.art: A tall coach standing up from a lawn chair and shouldering an aluminum bat, a teenager beside her, the late sun behind the dugout

failure.text: "Kid, I believe you believe it." She squints at you, worried now, which is worse than disbelief. "Come back tomorrow with something I can see. Then I'm all yours." She hands you an orange slice for the road.
failure.art: A coach holding out an orange slice to a teenager with a worried look, a ball field behind them

name: Dr. Amir Haddad
bio: Dr. Amir Haddad grew up in Dearborn, Michigan, the son of a Beirut tailor, and left a big Sacramento animal hospital after he refused to put down a dog that just needed time. Now he runs the Haddad Animal Clinic out of his garage on Crystal Street, charges what people can pay, and keeps meticulous case files on the strangest patients in California: a two-headed garter snake, a cat that glows faintly in the dark, a possum that talks in its sleep. He cooks enormous dinners for neighbors and is far too curious for his own good. His flaws: he avoids every fight with the homeowners' association, works until he falls asleep at the exam table, and is gentler with animals than with his own grief.

perk.name: Field Dressing
perk.text: Amir patches you up between scares, steady as a surgeon: once per night, cancel the nerve loss from one failed roll.

meet.title: The Crystal Possum
meet.place: The Haddad Animal Clinic, a garage on Crystal Street
meet.text: The garage door at number 9 is rolled up, and inside, under a hanging shop light, a man in a lab coat is bent over a wire cage. In it is a possum, and sprouting from its fur along its spine are tiny purple crystals, glittering like rock candy. "Found her under the roundabout this morning," Dr. Haddad says. "Third one this month. She's frightened, and she's very sick, and I don't have enough hands." A calico cat on his shoulder stares at you, unimpressed.
meet.art: A converted garage clinic under a hanging shop light, a veterinarian in a lab coat bent over a wire cage holding a possum with small purple crystals growing from its fur, a calico cat on his shoulder

choices.label: Glove up and hold the patient steady for the exam

success.text: You hold her gently while he works the crystals loose with tweezers, one by one, and she stops shaking under your hands. Dr. Haddad sits back and exhales. "You have good hands, and better nerve. I could use you. Out there, too, I think."
success.art: A teenager in oversized latex gloves gently holding a possum on an exam table while a veterinarian removes small purple crystals with tweezers

failure.text: She twists free and bites your thumb, not hard, but enough. Dr. Haddad cleans it, bandages it, and sends you home with a first-aid kit and an apology. "She's scared, not mean. Come back tomorrow. She'll remember you were kind."
failure.art: A veterinarian bandaging a teenager's thumb in a garage clinic, a possum glaring from its cage

choices.label: Read his case files and look for the pattern

success.text: You pin every strange case on his street map. Every single one was found within a block of the Heartstone, and they've doubled every Halloween week since 1981. Dr. Haddad takes off his glasses. "Then it isn't the animals that are sick. It's the street. We should look into this together."
success.art: A street map pinned on a garage wall with clustered red pins around a central roundabout, a teenager and a veterinarian studying it under a shop light

failure.text: The folders slide off the shelf and scatter across the floor. As you gather them, the calico cat fluffs to twice her size and hisses at an empty corner of the garage, steady and unblinking. Dr. Haddad turns off the light. "Tomorrow. Let's do this tomorrow."
failure.art: Case files scattered across a garage floor, a calico cat puffed up and hissing at a dark empty corner, a veterinarian reaching for a light switch

choices.label: Calm the possum by singing to her very softly

success.text: You sing the only lullaby you know all the words to, which is the theme from a cartoon about bears. The possum's ears relax. The cat purrs. Dr. Haddad laughs, quietly, so as not to break the spell. "Bedside manner. You can't teach that. Stay. Please."
success.art: A teenager singing softly beside a wire cage where a crystal-furred possum dozes, a veterinarian smiling and a calico cat purring on the counter

failure.text: Your voice cracks on the high note. The possum plays dead, deeply and theatrically. Dr. Haddad checks her pulse, then pats your shoulder. "She's fine. She's just a critic. Come back tomorrow and try a lower key."
failure.art: A possum dramatically playing dead in a cage with its tongue out, a teenager wincing, a veterinarian checking the animal with a stethoscope

name: Chip Merriweather
bio: Charles "Chip" Merriweather III is class president, captain of the debate team, organizer of every fundraiser at Glimmer Falls High and the son of the homeowners' association president, who sold half the houses on Crystal Street. He has a perfect GPA, a perfect side part and a smile for every photo. He has also known since junior high that he likes boys, and he has rehearsed saying so a hundred times to the bathroom mirror and never gotten past the first word. Chip is genuinely kind, sharp as a tack, a gifted organizer and a dork who makes terrible puns when he is nervous. His flaw is that he has spent so long being who everyone needs that he lies smoothly by reflex, and he is terrified of disappointing his father.

perk.name: Bake Sale Treasurer
perk.text: Chip runs every fundraiser in town and always rounds in the crew's favor: +1 quarter each dawn.
